extracted.intended_audience: students of the Royal Academy; painters and art students
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for painters (especially academy students) about style, hierarchy of excellences, imitation, medium, unity, and the appropriate relation between subject and manner. Emphasises pursuing the "higher excellences" first, consistency of style, and prudent use of subordinate or ornamental qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works built upon general nature endure
rubrics_metrics.description: The works, whether of poets, painters, moralists, or historians, which are built upon general nature, live for ever; while those which depend for their existence on particular customs and habits, a partial view of nature, or the fluctuation of fashion, can only be coeval with that which first raised them from obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer general, universal ideas over transient fashions; beware relying on particular customs or contemporary fashion since such works date quickly. Aim for qualities that transcend current taste to achieve lasting reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep principal attention on the higher excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: My advice in a word is this: keep your principal attention fixed upon the higher excellences. If you compass them and compass nothing more, you are still in the first class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise grand, elevated qualities (composition, majesty, correctness of form, energy) before pursuing lesser ornaments or minute elegancies. Being imperfect but possessing higher excellences is preferable to mastering only minor accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue subordinate qualifications only after higher ones
rubrics_metrics.description: If, when you have got thus far, you can add any, or all, of the subordinate qualifications, it is my wish and advice that you should not neglect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once core, higher qualities are secure, add secondary skills (colour niceties, fine finish) cautiously; do not let secondary aims displace primary excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uniting contrary excellences in one figure
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to unite contrary excellences (of form, for instance) in a single figure, can never escape degenerating into the monstrous, but by sinking into the insipid, taking away its marked character, and weakening its expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force incompatible qualities together; choose what can naturally co-exist. Combining opposing aims often yields incoherent or grotesque results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of passions is limited by beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: If you mean to preserve the most perfect beauty in its most perfect state, you cannot express the passions, which produce (all of them) distortion and deformity, more or less, in the most beautiful faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects and approaches consistent with preserving ideal beauty; highly expressive, passion-filled subjects may demand compromise of classical beauty and should be handled with awareness of that trade-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of affectation in pursuing grace and elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: They often boldly drive on to the very verge of ridicule; the spectator is alarmed, but at the same time admires their vigour and intrepidity... they have sometimes, perhaps, exceeded its boundaries, and have fallen into the most hateful of all hateful qualities, affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek grace and elegance, but avoid pushing them until they become artificial or ridiculous. Let vigour be balanced by restraint; study masters who avoid affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite style can improve the lower by borrowing the grand
rubrics_metrics.description: If a portrait painter is desirous to raise and improve his subject, he has no other means than by approaching it to a general idea... the lower may be improved by borrowing from the grand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elements of the grand style to elevate lesser genres, but be mindful: in portraiture, ennobling the sitter can sacrifice likeness. Balance dignity with required fidelity to the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and mode influence the excellence (fresco vs oil)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal works of modern art are in fresco, a mode of painting which excludes attention to minute elegancies: yet these works in fresco are the productions on which the fame of the greatest masters depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and prioritize works in the medium where higher excellences are best realized (e.g., fresco for grand compositions). Recognise that some media favour broad, elevated qualities while others lend themselves to finer niceties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the great models (Raffaelle, Michael Angelo, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raffaelle... owes his reputation... to his excellence in the higher parts of the art. Therefore, his works in fresco ought to be the first object of our study and attention... Michael Angelo claims the next attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct study time to capital works of acknowledged masters and their frescoes/canonical works to learn higher principles. Use these as primary models rather than minor or purely ornamental pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance breadth and nicety appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: He never acquired that nicety of taste in colours, that breadth of light and shadow... so as to make the object rise out of the ground with that plenitude of effect so much admired in the works of Correggio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for the right combination of broad handling (composition, light/shadow) and colour/nicety appropriate to your aims; study how masters balance these to avoid cramped or feeble effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: The summit is a proportioned assemblage of contrary qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The summit of excellence seems to be an assemblage of contrary qualities, but mixed, in such proportions, that no one part is found to counteract the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to combine multiple virtues in balanced proportion; mastery requires knowing how much of each quality to include so none overwhelms the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a particular walk to exercise all your powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose some particular walk in which you may exercise all your powers, in order each of you to be the first in his way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than scattering talents across many areas, specialize sufficiently to become preeminent in a chosen domain. Attempting everything risks mediocrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ornamental style sparingly to soften the great style
rubrics_metrics.description: I am of opinion that the ornamental style... may not be wholly unworthy the attention of those who aim even at the grand style; when it is properly placed and properly reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ ornament/venetian grace only to soften or mitigate harshness in the great style, not as a substitute for it. Emulate artists who incorporated ornament without overpowering their strength (e.g., Lodovico Caracci).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve unity and harmony across all parts of a work
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellency of every style... will very much depend on preserving that union and harmony between all the component parts, that they appear to hang well together, as if the whole proceeded from one mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency of manner, tone, and principles throughout a composition. Disparate excellences that do not cohere should be avoided; a work 'of a piece' shows true genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original/characteristical style requires internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: This I call the original or characteristical style; this... must be supported by the painter's consistency in the principles he has assumed, and in the union and harmony of his whole design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you pursue an idiosyncratic or original style, make sure its rules and principles are consistently applied so the whole reads as unified rather than merely eccentric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/portrait combinations must be complete and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: When a portrait is painted in the historical style... every circumstance ought to correspond to this mixture... if it is chosen it is necessary it should be complete and all of a piece: the difference of stuffs... should be distinguished in the same degree as the head deviates from a general idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If combining historical/antique manner with portraiture, match costume, pose, and treatment throughout; avoid mixing antique attitudes with modern dress or details that break the illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When painting antiquity, preserve the ancient air throughout
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainly when such subjects of antiquity are represented, nothing in the picture ought to remind us of modern times. The mind is thrown back into antiquity, and nothing ought to be introduced that may tend to awaken it from the illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anachronisms or modern elements when depicting classical or mythological subjects; ensure gestures, faces, drapery, and landscape support the period illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small excellences should be viewed, not obsessively studied
rubrics_metrics.description: Small excellences should be viewed, not studied; they ought to be viewed, because nothing ought to escape a painter's observation, but for no other reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe minor details to inform your practice, but do not devote disproportionate study to them at the expense of larger, governing principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective in whom you please and whom you imitate
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as select in those whom you endeavour to please, as in those whom you endeavour to imitate. Without the love of fame you can never do anything excellent; but by an excessive and undistinguishing thirst after it, you will come to have vulgar views; you will degrade your style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target refined patrons and models rather than pandering to popular taste. Excessive desire for popularity leads to degradation of style; choose exemplars and audiences that support higher aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware exhibitions seducing you to please the vulgar
rubrics_metrics.description: Our exhibitions... have also a mischievous tendency by seducing the painter to an ambition of pleasing indiscriminately the mixed multitude of people who resort to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exhibitions as opportunities for emulation and exposure, but resist allowing popular applause to dictate your artistic priorities or to tempt you into lower styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is necessary and productive of originality
rubrics_metrics.description: A painter must... be as necessarily an imitator of the works of other painters... imitation in the first stages of the art... may be extended throughout our whole life without any danger... I am... persuaded that by imitation only, variety, and even originality of invention is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace imitation of masters as an essential training method; even advanced artists benefit from studying predecessors. Imitation is a means to develop taste, variety, and eventual originality rather than a vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art has boundaries; do not attempt impossible romantic conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: What has been, and what can be done in the art, is sufficiently difficult; we need not be mortified or discouraged for not being able to execute the conceptions of a romantic imagination. Art has its boundaries, though imagination has none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the technical and expressive limits of the medium; adapt ambitious imaginative ideas to what painting can plausibly convey rather than forcing impossible conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to your powers and choose appropriate handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Guido, from want of choice in adapting his subject to his ideas and his powers, or in attempting to preserve beauty where it could not be preserved has in this respect succeeded very ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about your strengths and limits; select subjects that suit your abilities and avoid trying to force subject-matter that demands qualities you cannot convincingly supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: The great style excludes frantic search for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Such is the great style as it appears in those who possessed it at its height; in this, search after novelty in conception or in treating the subject has no place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pursue novelty for its own sake in works aiming for the grand style. Stability, timelessness, and adherence to higher principles matter more than capricious originality.
